anchor.quote: Use minimal punctuation to make meaning clear
Minimal punctuation doesn’t mean removing all punctuation marks from a sentence. It means removing unnecessary punctuation.
Only use punctuation that makes the sentence grammatically correct and the meaning clear.

not_rules.note: Broad, subjective advice for the writer.

anchor.quote: Too much punctuation makes text crowded and difficult to read. If a sentence has a lot of punctuation marks, it might be a sign that the sentence is too long or complex. Try to rewrite into shorter, clearer sentences.
To use minimal punctuation:
Minimal punctuation helps users understand your content.
Screen readers work best with minimal punctuation
Some screen readers will announce punctuation marks. Some will change the modulation of the voice depending on the punctuation mark.

By default, screen readers that people who are blind or have low vision use, do not usually announce punctuation. They may pause briefly when they encounter a comma, full stop, or semicolon. They may also change inflection when they encounter a question mark.
Screen readers usually ignore most other punctuation unless verbosity is set high, or a person reads character by character.
Watch out for misplaced punctuation: it can change meaning

anchor.quote: Use the correct spacing around punctuation marks
Check the relevant topic in this manual for advice on how to treat each punctuation mark.
There are different rules for putting spaces around punctuation marks. For example, some punctuation marks have no spaces around them. Some have a space on either side.
Capitalise the first word in a sentence and in headings
Use sentence case for:

anchor.quote: Proper nouns generally have an initial capital letter for each word in the noun.
Differences between proper and common names
This manual contains guidance for names and terms by topic. Always check a dictionary if in doubt.
Shortened forms
Use shortened forms only when this choice supports plain English.
Rules for capitalisation and punctuation differ from rules for terms spelt out in full. The rules depend on where the terms are in the sentence.
The spelt-out form might not need initial capitals, even if an acronym or initialism has them. Use normal capitalisation practices for proper and common nouns. If in doubt, check a dictionary.

not_rules.note: Restates rules on how to capitalise proper/common acronym expansions.

anchor.quote: Follow the guidance on capitals for titles and government terms

You do not need to use capitals when the title is an organisational name given to an office holder. Deference for positions within an organisation might follow house style. Do not use house style outside of the organisational context. Detail any special use of capitals in a style sheet.

not_rules.note: Relaxes title capitalisation requirements, and advises on house style.

anchor.quote: Preferences for capitals when the terms ‘traditional owner’, ‘elder’ and ‘custodian’ are used as titles should come directly from the relevant First Nations community.

Legal material has its own conventions for capitalisation. Content that has a legislative focus might use complementary sources to the guidance on citing legal material in this manual.
Punctuation and capitalisation have rules for correct use. Use minimal punctuation and capitalisation to make content more readable.

rules.quote: Don’t add full stops to the ends of headings, page headers, footers or captions.
rules.violation_condition: a full stop at the end of a heading, page header, footer or caption
rules.why: Clear and standalone negative instruction.

rules.quote: Don’t use a semicolon at the end of each item in a bullet list.
rules.violation_condition: a semicolon at the end of an item in a bullet list
rules.why: Clear and standalone negative instruction.

rules.quote: Unless each item is a full sentence or the last item in a list, don’t use a full stop for items in bullet lists.
rules.violation_condition: a bullet list item ending in a full stop that is neither a full sentence nor the last item in the list
when: each item is a full sentence
the item is the last item in a list
rules.why: Exceptions are recorded in 'when' as per G-2.

rules.quote: Don’t use full stops between letters in an acronym or initialism.
rules.violation_condition: full stops separating the letters of an acronym or initialism
rules.why: Clear and standalone negative instruction.

rules.quote: Don’t use a full stop at the end of most abbreviations.
rules.specification: Applies to most abbreviations; cross-check with the abbreviations list.
rules.violation_condition: a full stop at the end of an abbreviation that does not require one
rules.why: The word 'most' indicates exceptions exist, but the default is to flag.

rules.quote: Include a single space after a punctuation mark at the end of a sentence. Never use double spaces. Check each document for double and multiple spaces and delete them.
rules.violation_condition: two or more consecutive spaces after a punctuation mark at the end of a sentence, or elsewhere in the document
rules.why: Multiple sentences specifying the same core spacing prohibition.

rules.quote: Capitalise the first word in a sentence. Use lower case for all other words, unless those words include proper nouns. This is called ‘sentence case’.
rules.violation_condition: a sentence that does not begin with a capital letter, or contains capitalised words that are not proper nouns or other permitted exceptions
when: the word is a proper noun
rules.why: Core definition and requirement for sentence case.

rules.quote: opening quoted speech within a sentence
rules.violation_condition: opening quoted speech within a sentence that is not in sentence case
rules.why: Specific application of the sentence case rule to quoted speech.

rules.violation_condition: a heading that does not use sentence case
rules.why: Specific application of the sentence case rule to headings.

rules.quote: Do not use all capitals for headings, unless the visual design for the content meets WCAG in all respects.
rules.specification: Visual design exceptions are manual, but the check for all caps is automatable.
rules.violation_condition: a heading written entirely in capital letters
when: the visual design for the content meets WCAG in all respects
rules.why: Distinct rule regarding all-caps formatting, separate from standard sentence case.

rules.quote: Use sentence case with italics for titles of works mentioned in the content. This applies even when the reference is included in a heading within the content.
rules.violation_condition: a title of a work mentioned in the content that is not written in sentence case and italics
rules.why: Specific formatting rule for titles.

covers.quote: Minimise capitals for common nouns and adjectives

rules.quote: Common nouns and adjectives don’t use initial capitals, with few exceptions. For example, adjectives often have capitals when they refer to a national, religious or linguistic group.
rules.violation_condition: a common noun or adjective written with an initial capital letter
when: the adjective refers to a national, religious or linguistic group
rules.why: Consolidates heading and body text for uncapitalised common nouns.

examples.note: Compliant example of proper noun capitalisation.

parts.quote: ‘NSW’ is written out as ‘New South Wales’.

rules.quote: If the shortened form represents a proper noun, start each word with a capital letter.
rules.violation_condition: the spelt-out full form of a proper noun abbreviation written without initial capitals for each word
rules.why: Instruction for proper noun abbreviations.

examples.note: Compliant example showing common noun lowercase.

parts.quote: ‘EIS’ is written out as ‘environmental impact statement’.

rules.quote: If the shortened form represents a common noun, do not begin each word of the full form with a capital letter.
rules.violation_condition: the spelt-out full form of a common noun abbreviation written with initial capital letters
rules.why: Instruction for common noun abbreviations.

rules.quote: Only use capitals when the style is standardised or specified in regulations, for symbols of units of measurement.
rules.violation_condition: a symbol for a unit of measurement written with a capital letter where not standardised or specified in regulations
when: the style is standardised or specified in regulations
rules.why: Specific rule for unit symbols.

parts.quote: Chief Defence Scientist Tanya Monro presented the award ...

rules.quote: Follow conventions for using capitals for titles, honours and forms of address. Use capitals when an official title precedes the name of the office holder. This includes titles for executives specified in legislation.
rules.violation_condition: an official title preceding the name of the office holder that is not capitalised
rules.why: Instruction on capitalising titles preceding names.

parts.quote: The Senior Policy Adviser offered their view ...

rules.quote: Unless advised in this manual, avoid using capitals in body text for a particular position or role within an organisation. This practice goes against readability and does not support clarity.
rules.violation_condition: a position or role within an organisation capitalised in body text without preceding a name
rules.why: Instruction against title capitalisation when not preceding a name.

rules.quote: Legal documents often use initial capitals to show terms with a defined meaning (such as ‘Department’, ‘Schedule’, ‘Vendor’ and ‘Recipient’). In these cases, use the form of the name as it is written in the legislation.
rules.specification: Requires comparison against the legislation definitions.
rules.violation_condition: a term with a defined meaning in a legal document that is not capitalised as it is written in the legislation
when: the document uses terms with a defined meaning from legislation
rules.why: Specific rule for capitalising defined terms in legal texts.
